\chapter{How Much, and What to Call People}
\label{ch:fr-quantity}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say a lot, a little, very and enough, and address somebody the way French expects.}

Combien ? has had no possible answer since it was taught, and now it has four. The chapter also finishes the bare-de rule: a quantity word is already measuring, so the measuring article drops -- which is the same reason the partitive collapses after a negative, one chapter earlier.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[beaucoup]{beaucoup — \textquotedblleft{}a beautiful blow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C40-beaucoup}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{some} four ways and \emph{none} one way. You have no way at all to say \textbf{a lot}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the four partitives collapsing after a negative — \emph{pas de}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{beaucoup} — a lot, much, many.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{beaucoup de café} — a lot of coffee. · \textbf{beaucoup d'amis} — a lot of friends.
\end{quote}

Note what follows it: a bare \textbf{de}, exactly as after a negative. Any word of quantity in French takes \emph{de} and never \emph{du} or \emph{des}, for the same reason — the quantity word is already doing the measuring, so the measuring article drops out.

\textbf{beaucoup} is \textbf{beau} + \textbf{coup}, \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{beautiful blow}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Coup} is Latin \textbf{colaphus}, a punch on the ear, and English borrowed it far more politely as \emph{coup d'état} and \emph{a coup}. A word from a fistfight became the ordinary French for \emph{a lot} — the promotion any word earns by carrying emphasis often enough.

The \textbf{p} is silent, as final consonants are: \emph{boh-KOO}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{beaucoup} — \emph{boh-KOO}, the \emph{p} silent
  \item \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de pain\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup d'amis\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three shapes of the same \emph{de} — \textquotedblleft{}du café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}pas de café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de café\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two words inside it — \emph{beau} and \emph{coup}
  \item asked and explained — \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que c'est ? — Beaucoup de café, parce que j'ai beaucoup d'amis.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What follows \emph{beaucoup}? (\textbf{A bare \emph{de}} — never \emph{du} or \emph{des}.) Why? (\textbf{The quantity word is already measuring}, so the article drops.) What two words are inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Beau}} and \emph{\textbf{coup}} — a beautiful blow.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[un peu]{un peu — the other end of the scale}

\label{lesson:FR-C40-un-peu}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Beaucoup de café.} Say it, and say what has to follow any word of quantity.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{un peu} — a little.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{un peu de café} — a little coffee. · \textbf{un peu d'eau} — a little water.
\end{quote}

The same bare \textbf{de} follows it, because the same reasoning applies: the quantity is already stated.

\textbf{peu} is Latin \textbf{paucus}, \textquotedblleft{}few,\textquotedblright{} and English has it twice — in \textbf{paucity}, borrowed from the Latin directly, and buried in \textbf{poor}, which came through French from \emph{pauper}. So the everyday French word for \emph{a little} and the English word for \emph{scarcity} are one Latin adjective that travelled by two roads.

\textbf{un peu} is also the standard modest answer to a question about what you can do:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Vous parlez français ? — Un peu.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair, both ends of the scale — \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}un peu de café\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un peu de pain\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}un peu d'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the modest answer — \textquotedblleft{}Vous parlez français ? — Un peu.\textquotedblright{}
  \item asked short — \textquotedblleft{}C'est quoi ? — Un peu de pain.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What follows \emph{un peu}? (\textbf{A bare \emph{de}}, as after \emph{beaucoup}.) What Latin word is \emph{peu}? (\emph{\textbf{Paucus}}, \textquotedblleft{}few\textquotedblright{} — English \emph{paucity}.) Answer \emph{vous parlez français ?} modestly.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[très]{très — \textquotedblleft{}very,\textquotedblright{} and the line it crosses}

\label{lesson:FR-C40-tres}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Beaucoup} and \emph{un peu} measure a \textbf{thing} and both take \emph{de}. This one measures a \textbf{quality}, and it takes nothing at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{très} — very, in front of an adjective or an adverb.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{très bien} — very well. · \textbf{très bon} — very good.
\end{quote}

No \emph{de}, ever. That is the whole difference: \emph{beaucoup} and \emph{un peu} stand in front of a \textbf{noun} and need the bare \emph{de}; \emph{très} stands in front of an \textbf{adjective} and needs nothing.

\textbf{très} is Latin \textbf{trans}, \textquotedblleft{}across, beyond\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{trans} of \emph{transport} and \emph{translate}. To say a thing is \emph{très bon} is to say it has gone \textbf{across a line} into another category, which is what every intensifier in every language is trying to do.

The \textbf{s} is silent and comes back as a \textbf{z} before a vowel: \emph{très intéressant} is \emph{tray-zan-tay-ress-AHN}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}très bien\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}très bon\textquotedblright{}
  \item the feminine — \textquotedblleft{}très bonne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de café\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}très bon\textquotedblright{}
  \item the liaison — \textquotedblleft{}très intéressant\textquotedblright{}
  \item the answer everybody gives — \textquotedblleft{}Ça va ? — Très bien, merci.\textquotedblright{}
  \item as a command — \textquotedblleft{}Parle très bien !\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Écoute !\textquotedblright{}
  \item standing alone — \textquotedblleft{}Moi, très bien. Et toi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the weather, measured — \textquotedblleft{}Il fait très chaud.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Il pleut\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{le temps}, which is both the time and the weather
  \item the colours, measured — \textquotedblleft{}très vert\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}très jaune\textquotedblright{}, and the German cousin \emph{gelb} that \emph{jaune} is not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{très} stand in front of? (\textbf{An adjective or an adverb} — never a noun.) Does it take \emph{de}? (\textbf{No.}) What Latin word is it? (\emph{\textbf{Trans}}, \textquotedblleft{}across\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[assez]{assez — \textquotedblleft{}enough,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}rather\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C40-assez}



\begin{quote}
Three quantity words are yours. Two take \emph{de} and one does not. Say which is which before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{assez} — enough; and also \emph{rather}, \emph{fairly}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{assez de café} — enough coffee. · \textbf{assez bon} — rather good.
\end{quote}

It does both jobs, and which one it is doing depends on what follows it: before a \textbf{noun} it takes \emph{de} and means \emph{enough}; before an \textbf{adjective} it takes nothing and means \emph{rather}.

So \emph{assez} behaves like \emph{beaucoup} in one position and like \emph{très} in the other, which makes it the word that ties the chapter together.

\textbf{assez} is Latin \textbf{ad satis}, \textquotedblleft{}to enough.\textquotedblright{} That \emph{satis} is the root inside English \textbf{satisfy}, \textbf{saturate} and \textbf{satiate} — so to be \emph{satisfied} is literally to have been given \textbf{enough}.

The \textbf{z} is silent, like every final consonant, and unlike \emph{très} it does not usually come back before a vowel.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item with a noun — \textquotedblleft{}assez de café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}assez de pain\textquotedblright{}
  \item with an adjective — \textquotedblleft{}assez bon\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}assez bien\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four, in order of size — \textquotedblleft{}un peu, assez, beaucoup\textquotedblright{} and, for a quality, \textquotedblleft{}très\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin inside it — \emph{ad satis}, and English \emph{satisfy}
  \item about to happen — \textquotedblleft{}Je vais prendre assez de pain.\textquotedblright{}
  \item about him — \textquotedblleft{}Lui ? Assez bien.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does \emph{assez} take \emph{de}? (\textbf{Before a noun}, where it means \emph{enough}.) And when does it take nothing? (\textbf{Before an adjective}, where it means \emph{rather}.) What Latin phrase is it? (\emph{\textbf{Ad satis}} — \textquotedblleft{}to enough\textquotedblright{}.) Which English words share that root?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Monsieur, Madame]{Monsieur, Madame — \textquotedblleft{}my lord\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}my lady\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C40-monsieur}



\begin{quote}
You have said \textbf{bonjour} since page one and \textbf{vous} since the second chapter. A bare \emph{bonjour} to a stranger in France is slightly abrupt, and the word that fixes it is one you have never met.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Monsieur} — sir. · \textbf{Madame} — madam. · \textbf{Mademoiselle} — miss.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Bonjour, Monsieur.} · \textbf{Bonjour, Madame.}
\end{quote}

Two possessives fused into titles. \textbf{Monsieur} is \textbf{mon sieur}, \textquotedblleft{}my lord,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{Madame} is \textbf{ma dame}, \textquotedblleft{}my lady\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{dame} inside English \emph{dame} and \emph{damsel}, and the \emph{sieur} is a worn-down \emph{seigneur}, from Latin \textbf{senior}, \textquotedblleft{}the elder.\textquotedblright{}

The spelling records a word the mouth stopped saying centuries ago. \textbf{Monsieur} is pronounced \emph{muh-SYUH}: the \emph{n} has gone nasal-free, the \emph{s} is silent, and the ending is the \emph{eu} vowel. Nothing about the sound follows from the letters, which is why it is worth learning as a noise first and a spelling second.

Where English attaches a surname — \emph{good morning, Mr Dubois} — French attaches the bare title far more often. \textbf{Bonjour, Madame} to a shopkeeper is ordinary and expected; the surname is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the noise, not the spelling — \textquotedblleft{}Monsieur\textquotedblright{}, \emph{muh-SYUH}
  \item the greeting, completed — \textquotedblleft{}Bonjour, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Bonjour, Madame.\textquotedblright{}
  \item at night — \textquotedblleft{}Bonsoir, Madame.\textquotedblright{}
  \item thanking and leaving — \textquotedblleft{}Merci, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Au revoir, Madame.\textquotedblright{}
  \item introducing — \textquotedblleft{}Voici Madame Dubois.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two possessives inside them — \emph{mon sieur}, \emph{ma dame}
  \item closing a conversation — \textquotedblleft{}Je finis, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Nous finissons, Madame.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the courtesy words, each with a title — \textquotedblleft{}S'il vous plaît, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Je suis désolé, Madame.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Oui, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{}
  \item admitting it politely — \textquotedblleft{}Je ne comprends pas, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} and the stem it borrows from \emph{prendre}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words are inside \emph{Monsieur}? (\emph{\textbf{Mon}} and \emph{\textbf{sieur}} — \textquotedblleft{}my lord\textquotedblright{}.) And inside \emph{Madame}? (\emph{\textbf{Ma}} and \emph{\textbf{dame}}.) How is \emph{Monsieur} said? (\emph{Muh-SYUH} — the \emph{s} silent.) Greet a shopkeeper properly.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Combien ? — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:FR-R40-combien}



\begin{quote}
Four measures. Three take a bare \emph{de} in at least one position and one never does. Sort them, then say the one rule that decides it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the answers combien was waiting for}
\textbf{Combien ?} has had no answer since it was taught. Now it has four.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole table, measured — \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de café, un peu de lait, assez de pain, pas de vin\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup de fromage, un peu de sucre, assez de sel, pas de beurre\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the plural — \textquotedblleft{}beaucoup d'œufs\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}pas d'œufs\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four shapes of \emph{de} in one breath — \textquotedblleft{}du café, pas de café, beaucoup de café, un peu de café\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — qualities, measured}
Every adjective the book owns, intensified — and no \emph{de} anywhere.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}très bon, très bien, assez bon\textquotedblright{}
  \item the feminine — \textquotedblleft{}très bonne\textquotedblright{}, and the consonant it wakes
  \item the colours — \textquotedblleft{}très rouge, très blanc, assez noir, très vert\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the noun behind — \textquotedblleft{}un vin très rouge\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}un pain très blanc\textquotedblright{}
  \item the everyday exchange — \textquotedblleft{}Ça va ? — Très bien, merci.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: and the person you are talking to}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the greeting completed — \textquotedblleft{}Bonjour, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Bonsoir, Madame.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Merci, Madame.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Au revoir, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ? — C'est Madame Dubois.\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Voici Madame Dubois.\textquotedblright{}
  \item written, then as speech says it — \textquotedblleft{}Je ne sais pas, Monsieur.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Je sais pas.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four measures refuses \emph{de}? (\emph{\textbf{Très}}.) Which one takes it before a noun and not before an adjective? (\emph{\textbf{Assez}}.) Why do quantity words take a bare \emph{de} at all? (\textbf{They are already measuring}, so the measuring article drops.) And what two words are inside \emph{Monsieur}?
\end{tcolorbox}
